title: Distinguish railway inauguration, public availability and paid traffic
question: When did Bombay–Thane move from a ceremonial passenger trip to regular public service, and what evidence connects the project to its financial sponsor?
summary: The 8 April 1853 notice offered future fares for service starting 18 April. The 16 April invitation train carried passengers from Bori Bunder to Tannah. The Government Director records 18 April as the date the section opened for traffic, and the company revenue account starts the same day. A November 1853 newspaper summary gives 17 April and reports daily trains thereafter. The first ordinary train or ticket remains unresolved. A contract-and-accounts check supports an East India Company interest guarantee for the GIPR undertaking that included the first segment.
inputs: Candidate route, endpoints, alternate spellings and operator
Candidate opening date or date window
Dated period newspaper, timetable or company notice
Operator’s operating or traffic returns and account periods
Proposed source and destination of a financing or technology transfer

steps.title: Identify the route and its changing station names
steps.action: Search a period newspaper archive by operator and both endpoints, then use the first retrieved spelling variants in a railway timetable or official gazette repository. Search the heritage inventory and operator’s historical notices for dated station-name changes and verify the building date before joining sites.
steps.result: The ceremony report uses Boree Bunder and Tannah, modern Bori Bunder and Thane. ICOMOS places the later Victoria Terminus at Bori Bunder and dates its formal opening to 1887. The ministry dates the building’s start to 1878 and its name changes to 1996 and 2017. Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus identifies the modern site, and the current building postdates the 1853 trip.

steps.title: Read the offer and the ceremony account separately
steps.action: Search historical newspaper catalogues for the operator plus the endpoints and the terms opening, inauguration, fares and daily. Retrieve issues before and after the supposed opening. For each item record the publication date, event date, who could travel, and whether the writer reports a trip or advertises one. Trace reprints to the originating paper or catalogue and count duplicates as a single witness.
steps.result: The 8 April Bombay Times notice, inspected in later reproductions, advertises class fares and daily service from Monday 18 April. The Bombay Gazette account reprinted in Melbourne describes the 16 April ceremonial departure, guests, fourteen carriages and three unnamed engines. It gives a reported estimate of about 500 people. The modern Indian Railways account gives about 400. A separate Bombay Times report also describes an invitation event and nearly 500 attendees. These are estimates of the inaugural party. The original Trove page was unavailable during this run; the searchable Argus transcription preserves the newspaper report.

steps.title: Test public availability against traffic and annual accounts
steps.action: Search government and parliamentary report collections using the operator, year, receipts, working expenses, and opened for traffic. Look for a signed dated return, a section-opening table and passenger receipts or counts. Verify the scan and column headings, record start and end dates, and check whether the route grew during the accounting period.
steps.result: Danvers §41 dates the Bombay–Tannah opening to 18 April 1853, in a row grouped with the Mahim branch; it lists Tannah–Callian separately on 1 May 1854. Watt’s signed account starts 18 April 1853, as verified on the table itself; the appendix contents erroneously give 1858 for that start. The first row through 30 June 1854 gives £14,252 3s 8d total receipts across 34½ miles open. Danvers §142 separately reports 535,195 passenger conveyances and £13,647 passenger receipts in the year ending 30 June 1854. Those returns establish paid traffic during a period reaching beyond Bombay–Thane. Their shared company accounting limits their independence and their figures cannot be assigned to the first day.

steps.title: Seek a period source outside the accounts and preserve the alternative date
steps.action: Search period newspaper runs for the operator plus directors, half-yearly report and route variants. Compare a report close to the event with official dates, and search a local official gazette for carriage terms and changes to the schedule. Confirm digits in the scan. Distinguish first movement, first regular departure, public offer and the accounting start date.
steps.result: The Economist page image prints 17 April and reports two trains running daily thereafter, attributing both to the GIPR directors’ eighth half-yearly report. Searching that report title and the British Library company listings did not yield an inspected original. The independent newspaper publication relays the operator’s account. The 17 April date conflicts with Danvers’s 18 April date. The original directors’ report or a dated traffic log could clarify the discrepancy. The indexed Gazette points to a 26 April timetable notice reproduced on 11 August. Review of the page image, including stops and ticket terms, remains pending.

steps.title: Trace the financing at both ends
steps.action: For each proposed prerequisite or carrier, identify the actor and resource at the sending end and the receiving organisation, asset or section at the other. Search the corporate or government archive catalogue for the agreement, then match it against dated evidence of disbursement, repayment or use. Test whether another party supplied the capital or equipment and whether the documented contribution applied to the route.
steps.result: The sender was the East India Company acting as guarantor. The receiver was the Great Indian Peninsula Railway Company’s Bombay–Callian project, whose first opening was Bombay–Tannah. The British Library item identifies the August 1849 construction agreement, and Danvers §§36 and 41 identify the same undertaking and opening sequence. Danvers §48 records guaranteed interest received on capital raised in England and India, and the operator’s signed return records £7,122 4s 2d for the initial accounting period paid back to the East India Company in reduction of interest advanced. The 1853 share figures in The Economist and Danvers’s §44 identify investor capital alongside guaranteed interest. The original 1849 contract was located at catalogue level only; no exact rate for that original agreement or route-specific cost share is inferred.

steps.title: Decide the supported milestone and limit identity claims
steps.action: Record the earliest dated evidence for each milestone. Test any later commemoration against the contemporary account and seek an operating log, delivery record, or manufacturer’s serial number before assigning a locomotive or design lineage. Assign uncertainty at the level of the unresolved run, transaction, person or vehicle.
steps.result: Record 16 April as the invitation run and attribute the 18 April opening for traffic to Danvers. Preserve 17 April as an alternative reported date and the aggregate receipts as evidence of subsequent paid use. The Bombay departure remains Bori Bunder. The 1909 Gazetteer uses “opened for traffic” for 16 April and describes the public holiday and salutes. Read alongside the two period newspaper accounts of invitations and the operator’s 18 April accounting start, that phrase is insufficient to date ordinary paid service. The railway ministry’s anniversaries and postal issues mark the later station building. The period ceremony account describes three unnamed engines, which gives no specific join to the Merthyr Tramroad locomotive represented by steam-railway-traction.

decision: Add Danvers’s recorded opening for traffic on 18 April 1853. Keep the 8 April timetable as an offer, the contemporary report of 17 April as a conflicting date, and the later accounts as evidence of paid use during the reporting period. The first ordinary train or ticket remains unresolved. The accounts support the East India Company interest guarantee for the Bombay–Callian undertaking. Locomotive design transfer remains unresolved.
next: To resolve the one-day conflict, locate the original eighth half-yearly directors’ report or a dated station or traffic log for 17–18 April 1853. Search the British Library company minute books beginning at IOR/L/AG/46/12/2–29, checking the date range of each volume for the relevant meeting or report.
reject_if: Reject an exact first-day use claim based solely on a forward timetable, invitation ride, commemoration or the first row of a multi-date revenue account. Reject vehicle or design ancestry if records at the two ends give no common delivery, serial, drawing or personnel identifier.
stop_when: Record the strongest available stage once period operating or traffic evidence and an independently published check establish its scope. If published accounts conflict after the search of operating records and the nearest original company source is inaccessible, retain both dates with attribution and stop at the recorded opening rather than the first individual journey.
